mean: completely sure, with no doubt
ex: Rekha was certain she had locked the door, but she still walked back from the bus stop to check.
ex2: Are you certain the match starts at 7:30? The ticket in my hand says 7:00 in small print.
note: 'A certain person' means a particular person you don't name. 'For certain' = definitely: 'Nobody knows for certain.'

mean: probably going to happen or be true
ex: With dark clouds piling up over Marine Drive, heavy rain is likely by evening.
ex2: If the queue at the Aadhaar centre is this long at nine, it is likely we will not get a token today.
note: Use it with 'to': 'Prices are likely to rise.' 'Unlikely' is a polite way to say 'probably not'.

mean: easy to see or understand
ex: It was obvious from his muddy shoes that Kabir had played football in the rain instead of going to tuition.
ex2: From the crowd outside the Kolkata bakery, it was obvious that the Christmas plum cakes had just come out of the oven.
note: 'Obviously' can sound rude ('Obviously, you didn't read it'). Use it carefully with people who may not know.

mean: not easy to understand, or not yet known
ex: It is still unclear whether the Ganesh procession will take its usual route through the market this year.
ex2: After the meeting at the Bengaluru office, it was unclear who would actually send the report to the client.
note: 'It is unclear whether...' is the careful news way of saying the facts aren't in yet.

mean: to say or show that something is definitely true or fixed
ex: Please confirm your seat by tonight, or the travel agent will give the Goa ticket to someone else.
ex2: The hospital called to confirm Nani's cataract surgery for Monday morning at eight.
note: 'Kindly confirm once' is Indian English; in standard English just write 'Please confirm.'

mean: according to what you have heard, or what seems to be true
ex: Apparently the new biryani place near Charminar has a two-hour wait on Friday nights.
ex2: Apparently the panchayat has approved the new road, but nobody in the village has seen the official letter yet.
note: It signals you haven't checked it yourself. Spelling: double 'p', and '-ent' not '-ant'.

mean: having more than one possible meaning
ex: The sign 'No parking after 10' was ambiguous: nobody in the Chandigarh market knew if it meant morning or night.
ex2: Ravi's WhatsApp reply 'ok fine' was so ambiguous that his wife could not tell if he was angry or agreeing.
note: Ambiguous = more than one meaning; ambivalent = mixed feelings. Words are ambiguous; people feel ambivalent.

mean: to make a careful guess about a number or amount
ex: The contractor could only estimate the cost of fixing the leaking roof after the first heavy rain in Kochi.
ex2: The farmer could only estimate his wheat harvest until the crop was cut and weighed at the mandi.
note: The verb is ES-ti-mayt; the noun is ES-ti-mut. To 'underestimate' someone is to think they are weaker than they are.

mean: to guess about something without having enough facts
ex: Fans began to speculate about the captain's retirement when he skipped the post-match press conference.
ex2: It is too early to speculate about the cause of the fire at the Surat textile market.
note: News often says 'speculation is rife' (everyone is guessing). In money matters, to speculate is to make risky bets for profit.

mean: used to say you think something is probably true
ex: The lights at the Kapoors' flat are off, so presumably they have left for the wedding in Jaipur.
ex2: The results are already on the board's website, so presumably Tanvi knows her marks by now.
note: You are guessing sensibly from evidence. Related words: presume, presumption.

mean: not yet fixed or final; also done without full confidence
ex: The tentative date for Aditi's engagement is 14 February, but the pandit still has to check the muhurat.
ex2: Our group made a tentative plan for a Coorg trip, depending on whether the monsoon eases by then.
note: It can describe behaviour too: 'a tentative smile' is a shy, unsure one. Spelling: ten-ta-tive.

mean: to check that something is true or correct
ex: Before forwarding the 'breaking news' to the family group, Salma decided to verify it on two news sites.
ex2: The bank asked Mr Iyer to verify his new address with a recent electricity bill.
note: Verify = check whether it is true; confirm = state that it is true. You verify first, then confirm.

mean: used to say a claim is reasonable, though some may disagree
ex: Arguably, Sachin's 'Desert Storm' century in Sharjah was the finest one-day innings of the nineties.
ex2: Kolkata's puchka is arguably the best street snack in India, though Mumbaikars will always defend their pani puri.
note: It hedges a strong claim politely. It does not mean 'in an argumentative way'.

mean: in a way that is clear from what you can see
ex: Evidently, the bride's family had not expected two hundred extra guests; the caterer ran out of jalebis by nine.
ex2: Evidently the meeting had started early: by the time Neeraj logged in, everyone was already discussing the budget.
note: Evidently = clear from the evidence; apparently = it seems so, but you are less sure.

mean: possibly; in a way you can imagine happening
ex: If the Brahmaputra keeps rising, the ferry to Majuli could conceivably stop for a week.
ex2: With two wickets left and forty runs needed, Kerala could conceivably still win the Ranji Trophy match.
note: Weaker than 'probably': it only means 'not impossible'. Opposite idea: inconceivable.

mean: final and complete, accepted as the most reliable
ex: Dida's old notebook is the definitive guide to making shorshe ilish in our family.
ex2: Until the full report comes out, no one can give a definitive answer on what made the bridge collapse.
note: Definite = clear, fixed ('a definite yes'). Definitive = final, the standard ('the definitive biography'). Not interchangeable.

mean: proving something so clearly that no doubt is left
ex: The blood test gave conclusive proof that Imran's fever was typhoid, not dengue.
ex2: The CCTV footage from the ATM was not conclusive, because the thief had covered his face with a scarf.
note: Conclusive is about proof ending the doubt; definitive is about being the final, standard version.

mean: doubting that something is true or will work
ex: Many farmers in Vidarbha were sceptical of the new seed until they saw their neighbour's harvest.
ex2: Ammi was sceptical of the TV advert that promised one cream would remove every wrinkle in a week.
note: British/Indian spelling 'sceptical', American 'skeptical'; both have a hard 'k'. Sceptical is healthy doubt; cynical assumes the worst.

mean: not giving a clear result or answer
ex: Talks between the two housing societies over the shared park were inconclusive, so they will meet again on Sunday.
ex2: The first round of tests was inconclusive, so the doctor at AIIMS asked Mohan to repeat them after a week.
note: An 'inconclusive' test result means 'we still don't know', not 'negative'.

mean: completely clear, leaving no doubt at all
ex: The principal's message was unequivocal: no phones in the exam hall, not even switched off.
ex2: The coach's support for the young spinner was unequivocal, even after he gave away twenty runs in his first over.
note: Spelled 'unequivocal', never 'unequivocable'. Adverb 'unequivocally' is common: 'She unequivocally denied it.'

mean: probably not true, honest or good; or feeling doubtful about something
ex: The 'government job' offer that asked for fifty thousand rupees upfront looked dubious to Rahul's mother.
ex2: Meera's excuse of 'urgent work' looked dubious when neighbours heard loud cricket commentary through her door during the society meeting.
note: A thing is dubious (suspect); a person is dubious about something (unsure). 'Dubious distinction' = an honour you'd rather not have.

mean: arranged for now, and likely to be changed or confirmed later
ex: Neha got provisional admission to the Delhi college, subject to her final marksheet arriving by August.
ex2: The provisional voter list is pinned outside the panchayat office so people can point out mistakes before it is final.
note: Tentative = uncertain; provisional = officially 'for now' until confirmed, as in a provisional certificate.

mean: as it seems or is claimed, though the real reason may be different
ex: Ostensibly Mamaji came to return the pressure cooker, but he really wanted to discuss a match for his son.
ex2: Ostensibly the startup's founders went to Goa for a 'strategy offsite', but most of their photos were from the beach.
note: It hints the stated reason is not the real one. Apparently = it seems so; ostensibly = that's the claim, but doubt it.

mean: unclear, often on purpose, so it can be read more than one way
ex: Asked whether fees would rise, the college trustee gave an equivocal reply about 'reviewing all options'.
ex2: When her father asked if she would join the family business, Zoya gave an equivocal answer and quickly changed the subject.
note: Ambiguous may be accidental; equivocal suggests dodging. The verb 'equivocate' means avoid giving a straight answer.

mean: at first look, before checking more deeply
ex: The magistrate said there was a prima facie case against the builder for using poor-quality cement.
ex2: Prima facie, the cheaper flat in Thane looked like a good deal, until the broker mentioned the daily water shortage.
note: Legal Latin, very common in Indian court reports. Prima facie evidence can still be disproved later. No hyphen.

mean: able to happen or be true, but not sure
ex: It is possible that the Rajdhani will be late because of the fog, so pack some extra food.
ex2: Doctors said it was possible that Sunil's cough came from the dust at the building site next door.
note: 'Possible' = it may happen; 'probable' = it will most likely happen. Say 'more likely', not 'more possible'.

mean: to think something is probably not true or will not happen
ex: I doubt the plumber will come today; it's Holi and the whole street is shut.
ex2: Coach Bhatia never let the girls doubt that they could beat the bigger school in the final.
note: Indian English says 'I have a doubt' for 'I have a question'; elsewhere 'doubt' means you think it is untrue. The b is silent.

mean: without any doubt; for sure
ex: Ma, I will definitely call you when the bus reaches Shimla.
ex2: This is definitely the best dosa in Matunga; I have tried every stall on the street.
note: Spelt -ite-, not -ate-: 'definately' is one of the commonest spelling mistakes.

mean: not sure, or not yet known
ex: With the cycle factory closing down, Bablu's future in Ludhiana looked uncertain.
ex2: Sneha was uncertain whether to take science or commerce after Class 10, so she spoke to three teachers.
note: 'Unclear' is about facts nobody knows yet; 'uncertain' can also describe a person who cannot decide.

mean: a story people pass on that may not be true
ex: A rumour spread on WhatsApp that schools would shut for a week, but the district office denied it.
ex2: There is a rumour in the office that the whole Hyderabad team will move to the new building in March.
note: British and Indian spelling is 'rumour'; American is 'rumor'. 'Rumour has it that...' is a common opening.

mean: to think something is probably true, without proof
ex: I suspect the milkman has been adding water; the tea has tasted thin all week.
ex2: Doctors suspect the stomach bug came from the water tank at the hostel in Manipal.
note: Verb: suh-SPEKT. Noun, a person police think did a crime: SUS-pekt. 'I suspect' politely softens a guess.

mean: a feeling that something is true, without clear reasons
ex: Ritu had a hunch her brother was planning a surprise party, because he kept hiding his phone.
ex2: On a hunch, the old fisherman in Ratnagiri took his boat further south and came back with a full catch.
note: Informal. In a report, write 'I suspect' or 'my early guess is' instead.

mean: said to be true, but not yet proved
ex: The chemist allegedly sold fake medicines, but the case is still in court.
ex2: Our neighbour's dog allegedly ate the whole box of laddoos, though nobody actually saw it happen.
note: News reports use it to report a charge without calling someone guilty before a court decides.

mean: very hard to believe; unlikely to be true
ex: Mohan's excuse that a monkey ran off with his homework sounded far-fetched, even in Shimla.
ex2: A metro line to our small town once seemed far-fetched, but the survey team arrived last month.
note: Keep the hyphen. 'Not so far-fetched' is a useful way to say an odd idea may be right.

mean: not certain; people can fairly disagree about it
ex: Whether Kapil Dev or Dhoni was the better captain is debatable, and our hostel argued about it till 2 a.m.
ex2: It is debatable whether the costly coaching classes helped Arpit more than his own self-study did.
note: Calling a claim debatable is a polite way to say you doubt it.

mean: not yet checked or proved to be true
ex: The channel showed an unverified video of the flood, and later admitted it was from another state.
ex2: Grandpa forwards every unverified health tip to the family group, like raw garlic curing diabetes.
note: Not the same as false: an unverified story may be true, but nobody has checked it yet.

mean: very clear and firm, leaving no doubt at all
ex: The hospital gave a categorical assurance that no patient would be turned away for lack of money.
ex2: Ishaan gave a categorical denial about the broken window, though his cricket ball lay on the floor.
note: Often used as 'categorically': 'The company categorically denied the report.' Stronger than 'clearly'.

mean: very weak; hardly enough to convince anyone
ex: The case against the young clerk was tenuous: one blurry photo and some office gossip.
ex2: The link between the cricket captain's lucky socks and the team's wins is tenuous at best.
note: Used for links, claims and holds, as in 'a tenuous grip'. Not used for a physically weak person.

mean: claimed to be true or real, though it may not be
ex: A purported letter from the university announcing a holiday turned out to be fake.
ex2: The purported cure for baldness sold at the Sunday market in Pune was just coconut oil with perfume.
note: News uses it for clips or papers not yet confirmed: 'a purported audio clip'. 'Alleged' is used more for crimes.

mean: (of a story) told by many people but probably not true
ex: The family story that great-grandfather once chased off a tiger with a lathi is almost certainly apocryphal.
ex2: Every hostel has an apocryphal legend, like the senior who topped his finals after sleeping through the paper.
note: Use it for stories, quotes and anecdotes. Many 'quotes' from Gandhi or Einstein on WhatsApp are apocryphal.

mean: how true or accurate something is
ex: Before printing the story, the editor asked a reporter in Patna to check the veracity of the leaked papers.
ex2: The judge questioned the veracity of the witness, who had changed his story twice.
note: Formal. Do not confuse it with 'voracity', which means a huge hunger.
